comments.author: @tonyzeh
comments.text:
Capitalism is what killed the dream. At its core, capitalism depends on exploitation, though many people don't recognize it. The system relies on keeping workers in vulnerable positions so businesses can maximize profits from their labor.

One example is education. Higher education is not free in the United States, which means many young people begin their adult lives burdened with debt. That debt limits their freedom because it must be repaid regardless of their circumstances. As a result, people often take whatever job they can find just to stay afloat. Employers benefit from the education workers paid for themselves, yet wages often fail to reflect the time, effort, and debt invested in obtaining that education.

Healthcare is another example. In many countries, healthcare is treated as a right. In the United States, millions of people struggle to maintain health insurance that often comes with high monthly costs, deductibles, and out-of-pocket expenses. Even then, a medical emergency can still lead to financial hardship. Because healthcare is frequently tied to employment, employers gain another form of leverage over workers.

At the same time, regulations often fail to adequately address unhealthy food systems and other factors that contribute to poor public health. More illness means more hospital visits and greater dependence on expensive pharmaceuticals. From this perspective, capitalism profits from every stage of the cycle.

Critiquing capitalism does not mean opposing private ownership, entrepreneurship, or the exchange of goods and services. It means challenging a system that allows people to accumulate enormous wealth by exploiting the labor and circumstances of others. The goal is not to prevent people from owning businesses, but to prevent exploitation and ensure that the people whose work creates value receive a fair share of the benefits.
